theme: The Day of the LORD; the LORD rejoices over his people
readingInstruction: Read Zephaniah 1:1-3:20. The last of this unit’s prophets begins with a terrifying announcement of the Day of the LORD and ends with one of the most tender images of God in the Bible. Read the last four verses twice.
settingTheScene: Zephaniah prophesied in the days of King Josiah, around 640 to 609 BC, before Josiah’s reforms took hold. His great-grandfather was Hezekiah, so he may have been of royal blood. The book is built around the phrase “the day of the LORD.” It begins with a universal judgment, calls Judah to repent, speaks against the nations, and ends with restoration. It prepares the way for the exile that is coming.
observation: “I will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth, declares the LORD” (1:2).
“The great day of the LORD is near, near and hastening fast” (1:14).
“Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD” (2:3).
“Woe to her who is rebellious and defiled, the oppressing city!” (3:1).
“She listens to no voice; she accepts no correction. She does not trust in the LORD; she does not draw near to her God” (3:2).
“For at that time I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD” (3:9).
“But I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the LORD” (3:12).
“The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (3:17).
interpretation:
The first chapter is relentless. God will sweep away everything: man and beast, birds and fish. The reason is idolatry and spiritual indifference. The people worship Baal and the host of heaven, and others say in their hearts, “The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill.” They are practical atheists who believe that God does nothing. God will search Jerusalem with lamps. The day is described as a day of wrath, distress, ruin, darkness, and gloom. Not even silver or gold can deliver them.

Then chapter 2 begins with a call: “Gather yourselves together… before the decree takes effect… seek the LORD, all you humble of the land.” The only protection is humility and a search for righteousness. “Perhaps you may be hidden.” The word “perhaps” reminds us that no one deserves to be saved. Yet the invitation is real. The remaining part of the chapter pronounces judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria. Nineveh will be a desolation.

Chapter 3 returns to Jerusalem, “the oppressing city,” which did not listen or trust. Officials are roaring lions, judges evening wolves, prophets reckless and treacherous, priests profane the sanctuary. “The LORD within her is righteous; he does no injustice.” God had hoped that she would learn, but she was eager to make her deeds corrupt.

And then the turn, “For at that time.” The nations will call on the name of the LORD. A humble and lowly remnant will be left, who do no injustice and speak no lies. They will lie down with none to make them afraid. Then the song: “Sing aloud, O daughter of Zion.” The reason is verse 17, one of the most beautiful verses in the Old Testament. The LORD is in your midst, a warrior who saves. He rejoices over you with gladness. “He will quiet you by his love.” He sings over you. The God who judged is the God who sings. The same hand that sweeps away the proud gathers the humble.
connection: Jesus is the one in the midst of his people who saves (Matthew 1:21; 18:20). Romans 8:1 says there is no condemnation for those in Christ, who have been hidden on the day of wrath. Luke 15:5-7 and 15:20-24 show heaven rejoicing over sinners who return. Hebrews 12:22-24 describes the gathered assembly of the firstborn. Revelation 7:9-17 shows the multitude from every nation, with God wiping away tears. 1 Thessalonians 1:10 says Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come.
application:
Read Zephaniah 3:17 aloud, replacing “you” with your own name, and sit in it for a few minutes.

Ask whether you ever live as if “the LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill,” as a practical atheist.

Pray for humility, the posture that Zephaniah says leads to being hidden.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to hide you in the day of his anger.
Tell him you seek righteousness and humility.
Thank him that he rejoices over you with singing.
